A1.justification: Both PDFs describe HyperMARL. Their complete main texts and appendices support comparison, and retained methods, equations, tables and figures can be matched despite substantial restructuring.

before.justification: v2 reports original REINFORCE game experiments, MARL benchmark evaluations, policy-diversity measurements and component ablations.

after.justification: v3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds temporal-game results, gradient-conflict measurements, MATD3 comparisons and computational-efficiency measurements.

M1.justification: The agent-conditioned linear/MLP hypernetworks, embeddings, initialization and gradient-decoupling architecture remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 matches after spelling and formatting normalization. The MATD3 experiments apply HyperMARL with another backbone without introducing a new HyperMARL component.

E1.justification: v3 adds temporal Specialisation and Synchronisation games in which agents observe previous joint actions, plus the Swimmer-v2-10x2 locomotion scenario. The existing Dispersion, Navigation, other MAMuJoCo scenarios and SMAX coverage remain.

E2.justification: Kaleidoscope changes from explicitly excluded in v2 Table 7 to an evaluated comparator in v3 Table 5, alongside independent-actor MATD3, across four MAMuJoCo scenarios. v3 Figure 4 also introduces the FuPS+ID (No State) comparator. Renaming existing FuPS baselines to FuPS+ID does not add a method: v2 already specifies ID conditioning.

E3.justification: v3 introduces off-policy MATD3 evaluation alongside the retained PPO experiments. Its temporal-game protocol uses 10-step episodes, batch size 32 and periodic 100-episode evaluations, whereas v2 documents static-game trials with batch size 10. Normal-form tests extend to 32 agents, and new inference/memory benchmarks introduce controlled network, batch and environment configurations.

E4.justification: v3 adds direct inter-agent gradient-conflict analysis with a no-state control and measures inference-speed and GPU-memory scaling beyond the existing parameter-count study. Conversely, v2's Humanoid hidden-size and one-hot-embedding ablations disappear; their Dispersion counterparts remain. The gradient-decoupling and initialization ablations in both environments are retained and redisplayed.

E5.justification: v3 reports 10 Dispersion seeds versus five in v2, although v3 Table 7 still lists only five seed IDs. Game reporting changes from mean±SD tables to 10-seed 95% CIs for temporal games and standard errors for normal-form games. The timing study specifies 10 independent trials. Existing MARL bootstrap-CI reporting largely continues.

E6.justification: v3 adds temporal-game returns, gradient-conflict outcomes, MATD3 returns and speed/memory results, and replaces the earlier normal-form game tables with expanded curves. Its new Swimmer comparison reports IQMs of 465.91 for HyperMARL and 462.48 for Kaleidoscope, with overlapping CIs. All numerical entries in v2's MAPPO MAMuJoCo Table 4 are retained in v3 Table 2; the off-policy results are separate evaluations.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix F.2 extends the existing gradient factorization with an explicit estimator, covariance expansion and assumptions of independent trajectories, finite second moments and fixed parameters during differentiation. Appendix E formalizes general-n rewards and temporal games. The specialization definition and two-player impossibility proof remain; the added covariance identity does not establish a comparative variance bound.

C1.justification: The central contribution and adaptability claims remain: agent-conditioned hypernetworks support diverse behaviours without changing the RL objective or prescribing diversity. v3 adds a more explicit abstract/introduction claim that coupling observations and agent IDs exacerbates gradient conflict, strengthening v2's primarily variance-based motivation.

C2.justification: v3 substantially expands the mechanism explanation through observation–ID interference and deterministic gradient transformations. It also corrects v2's broad initialization-necessity interpretation: initialization matters strongly in Humanoid but has little effect in Dispersion. New runtime tradeoffs are discussed. However, Figure 13's claim that FuPS+ID retains near-optimal specialization performance conflicts with its pronounced decline at 32 agents.

D1.justification: v2 promises future code availability; v3 reports public availability and supplies a repository link. v3 additionally documents hardware, per-run execution times and aggregate compute hours in Appendix J, the runtime-benchmark configuration, and MATD3/Kaleidoscope implementation details. These are substantial reproducibility disclosures; repository availability was not externally verified.

R1.justification: v3 adds references on universal approximation, game theory and empirical RL design, while dropping the Cho and Engstrom references. Kaleidoscope, already cited in v2, becomes an evaluated competitor. The principal related-work organization and positioning against QMIX, CASH and parameter-sharing approaches remain.

P1.justification: The introduction, motivating experiments, experimental narrative and ablation discussion are extensively rewritten. Embeddings and initialization subsections are merged, the specialization definition moves to an appendix, and the appendices are substantially reorganized. The author list also adds Amos Storkey.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one. Dispersion curves, gradient variance and diversity are consolidated; the numerical diversity table becomes a bar chart, and interval plots move to the appendix. New game diagrams, conflict plots, runtime plots and an off-policy table are added. Ablation figures are reorganized, and some interval-plot labels become crowded.

improvement.justification: v3 strengthens mechanistic and comparative evidence through direct gradient-conflict controls and the previously excluded Kaleidoscope comparison, while adding useful computational and reproducibility information. It also better qualifies initialization effects. These gains are tempered by removed Humanoid ablations, inconsistent Dispersion seed documentation and Figure 13's misleading near-optimal-performance caption. The net quality improvement is useful but limited.
